en: *Weiriruzhannjing* (The Sutra on the Daily Intermingling of Difficulties), one fascicle;
translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty.
At the beginning, the Bodhisattva Cheli receives the Way. "Cheli" means that for the sake of receiving and practicing, one advances upward to [the stage of] *A*... [text fragment].
Only those who have attained *avaivartika*—the state of non-retrogression—are those whose minds no longer turn back;
next are the *bodhivīra* bodhisattvas, the first of whom are the flying bodhisattvas;
next are the bodhisattvas who act as Buddhas, the first of whom are called *puruṣadamyasārathi*, also known as "men of the Way."
The practice of a bodhisattva also issues from twelve gates; because they sever the three evil paths, they are born before the Buddhas of the ten directions and not in the tenth heaven above.
A srotāpanna likewise issues from twelve gates and severs the three evil paths, but is born in the tenth heaven above.

Although both emerge from the twelve gates, the reason they are not born in the same place is that the *srotāpanna* possesses sixteen mental states, whereas the bodhisattva practices thirty-four mental states; for this reason, they are not born in the same place.
The Bodhisattva practices thirty-four mental states: namely, the sixteen mental states of the Four Truths and the eighteen unique practices; these combined constitute the thirty-four mental states.
The Bodhisattva, by practicing these thirty-four mental states, is able to master everything;
the Arhat practices sixteen mental states.
The Bodhisattva possesses great power and explains all things through his mastery;
from the Srotāpanna up to the Arhat, they sever their fetters face-to-face upon encountering an object.

Having perfected the thirty-four mental applications through sitting and walking meditation, one then attains the sixteen mentalities of a Buddha, each ranging from the first to the sixteenth according to its respective category.
The same applies to the four dhyānas.
A bodhisattva practicing with diligence for twenty kalpas could attain Buddhahood;
however, because there are three [deficient] intentions, he does not attain Buddhahood.
What are these three?
They are the intention of a Buddha, the intention of a pratyekabuddha, and the intention of an arhat; because of these three intentions, one does not attain Buddhahood.

This means that one attains according to what is most predominant: if one is predominantly a Buddha, one attains Buddhahood; if predominantly a Pratyekabuddha, one attains Pratyekabuddhahood; and if predominantly an Arhat, one attains Arhatship—just as a scale inclines toward whichever side is heavier.
Among those who dwell at home, there are some who attain the state of Arhat, Anāgāmin, Sakṛdāgāmin, or Srotāpanna; there are also those who attain the stage of an Avaivartika Bodhisattva.
There are four reasons why he abandoned his home and entered the mountains:
first, he feared people would say, "The Bodhisattva is lustful; how could he have attained the Way?"

Second, even the wheel-turning kings of gold must all renounce their kingdoms; third, Māra will come to harass the Bodhisattva; fourth, one who seeks the Buddha-way does not remain in the household life.
Having received the prediction (vyākaraṇa), a bodhisattva who severs new karmic receptions and practices with diligence shall attain Buddhahood after one hundred kalpas;
whereas for those who do not practice with diligence, it may take a long time to attain it, or they may not attain it at all, as there is no fixed limit to their duration.

Because a bodhisattva who has received a prophecy repays [their debts], they do not create new ones; that is to say, from the time of receiving the prophecy onward, they repay the offenses committed in previous lives as well as those committed in the present life before receiving the precepts, and they repay all offenses from incalculable eons as well.
From the bodhisattvas who have received their predictions down to the srotāpannas, all possess past offenses.
Sometimes they encounter these old offenses, and because they follow them into rebirth, their aspiration for the Way becomes thin.
If someone says that the meaning of the profound sutras is to understand transgressions and blessings as being like a pointing gesture or like something that does not arise again— that is,
because a person no longer commits transgressions, they are finished— and that a bodhisattva receives their prediction (vyākaraṇa) after a hundred kalpas and then attains Buddhahood.
Regarding the statement that Śākyamuni Buddha had already completed ninety-one kalpas, it is because through his diligence he attained ninety kalpas.
This is analogous to a person who is to travel a thousand li tomorrow; if they travel nine hundred li today, the distance covered is equal in calculation.

When one counts from the ninety-first kalpa up to the hundredth kalpa, the signs of an avaivartika bodhisattva are finally perfected; having completed the causes over a hundred kalpas, it does not exceed a hundred kalpas. Without attaining the state of an avaivartika bodhisattva, the characteristics of such practice are not yet accomplished.
If a person gives rise to the thought of the Way, its merit surpasses the evils of a hundred thousand kalpas.
What is the thought of the Way?
To keep one's mindfulness fixed upon the Four Noble Truths—this is the thought of the Way.
Evil is like darkness, and the aspiration for the Way is like light; just as when the sun rises, the darkness of the world is extinguished.
When the bodhisattvas heard these words, they all rejoiced greatly, saying, "Namo Buddha," and by giving rise to this single thought of goodness, they obtained blessings for a hundred kalpas.

When a bodhisattva offers his own body to feed a starving tigress, instead of requiring one hundred kalpas, he becomes a Buddha in ninety-one kalpas; this is because, by not perceiving the pain, he eliminates nine kalpas.
When a bodhisattva has already resolved to revile his own person and also to revile the persons of others, this constitutes "reviling both.
When the Buddha was a bodhisattva, he did not revile others.
For what reason is it called "shame" (dhu)?
When one is called by name, one immediately becomes agitated; this is suffering and unpleasant, and to experience it oneself is what is meant by "shame."
One who practices calamity and perishes from the ground of merit—for this reason, others further recite and proclaim that long-standing calamities have exhausted their roots of goodness;

this is what is meant by "self-reproach. Not knowing and not seeing, how could one see the path of others? Having already reproached others for their intentions, one should immediately, through these causes and conditions, reproach oneself in two ways.
Now, in this present life, both others and oneself are ill at ease; for this reason, one must exclaim, "Alas!

When a practitioner of the Way recognizes that such poison has arisen, they should restrain it while remaining within the cycle of birth and death. For if this poison arises, it will become a long-lasting calamity and will shroud the roots of goodness.
There are five practices for a bodhisattva:
first, rising early; second, waiting for the proper time; third, not offending others; fourth, constant mindfulness; and fifth, repeated practice.
What is meant by "rising early"?
It means being diligent and mindful of the Path.
What is meant by "waiting for the proper time"?
This means that when someone who is worthy of receiving a gift arrives, if they come with a benevolent mind, one should immediately give it to them and act accordingly.
What is meant by "not offending others"? It means being able to benefit all people.
What is constant mindfulness?

It means desiring to bring benefit to others; desiring to resolve the difficulties of those facing official legal proceedings; desiring to cure those who are ill; and desiring to give alms to the poor.
What is meant by "reciprocity"?
To receive an object worth a single coin from another person, yet desire to repay it a hundredfold or a thousandfold—this is reciprocity.
A bodhisattva encounters the cycle of birth and death, yet while there is no actual phenomenon of birth and death, there is the intention regarding birth and death.
Arhats sever the world and sever their intention;
Bodhisattvas sever the world but do not sever their intention. The reason they do not sever their intention is that they shall attain the Buddha-way in order to deliver the people of the world.
The Bodhisattva fears worldly affairs and discourses; because he does not transgress them, he abandons worldly affairs.
The Bodhisattva severs the intention for birth and death, yet does not sever the activities of birth and death; that is to say, while remaining in the world, he merely refrains from committing evil.
The Bodhisattva only severs the five sensory faculties but does not sever the mind. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva’s mind is conjoined with birth and death, he does not sever the mind; it is because he desires to deliver the people of the ten directions.

The reason why Bodhisattvas practice giving, maintain the precepts, leave the household life, cultivate wisdom, exert diligence, practice patience, attain sincerity, possess courage, maintain mindfulness of the good, and exercise discernment is that by upholding these ten matters, they attain the wisdom of a Buddha.

When a bodhisattva is born into a poor family, they should maintain the precepts; when in a wealthy family, they should practice giving; when in a noble family, they should practice patience; and when in the mountains, they should practice meditation.

This is why a bodhisattva employs the four foundations of mindfulness and the seven factors of enlightenment: once the four foundations of mindfulness are attained, one then attains the seven factors of enlightenment.
When the Bodhisattva went out on his journey, he saw four sights:
first, he saw an old man; second, he saw a sick man; third, he saw a dead man; and fourth, he saw suffering.
Seeing that time is pressing, one practices the Path; yet people daily move toward death—why then do they not fear the moment of death?
For what reason? Because they fear its arrival.
Once the Bodhisattva has attained the Way of the Buddha, he then expounds the Four Noble Truths.
Why is this? There are four causes and conditions for expounding the Four Noble Truths:
First, because of that which has never been heard before; second, because of the use of dhyāna; third, because of the use of obtaining the eye; fourth, because of the use of obtaining wisdom.
Because one cannot escape the great prison due to old age, sickness, death, and sorrow, the Four Noble Truths are taught.
There are four causes and conditions for a Bodhisattva to preach a sutra:
first, the king’s approval; second, what people delight in; third, their receptive minds; and fourth, the proper time.
What is the proper time?
It is when people are inclined to listen.
The Bodhisattva reflects for himself:
"By what causes and conditions does suffering arise?
[He reflects: "It arises from birth.
By what conditions does birth arise?"
It is obtained from volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). By what cause and condition are volitional formations obtained?
They are obtained from ignorance (*avidyā*).
By what causes and conditions does delusion arise?
It arises from craving.
By what causes and conditions does craving arise?
From the practice of receiving [the teachings], one neither receives nor attains them.
A bodhisattva regards a hundred kalpas as a single night. Why is this?
Ordinary people cannot endure illness for even a single day, yet a Bodhisattva endures pain for a hundred kalpas as if it were a single day of illness for a person.
Sometimes, when practicing the Way for a single day, the merit thereof remains inexhaustible after a hundred kalpas; therefore, it is said that he regards a hundred kalpas as a single night.
At other times, when the Bodhisattva turns his practice toward preaching the sutras with no concern for birth and death, he regards a hundred kalpas as a single night.
A bodhisattva who has not yet attained the Way of the Buddha does so for three reasons:
first, not encountering virtuous people; second, having no causes, conditions, or material resources for what one wishes to do; and third, failing to deliberate upon right and wrong.
It is because of these matters that they have not attained the Way.
There are three matters by which a bodhisattva sitting [in meditation] fails to attain the Way of the Buddha:
first, dwelling in the world for a long time without awakening; second, failing to encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra); and third, failing to extinguish and eliminate distracted thoughts.
A bodhisattva fails to attain the Way due to three circumstances:
first, not hearing [the Dharma]; second, the absence of self-generated intention; and third, lacking a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra).

A bodhisattva both enters into transgression and emerges from it; when the mind follows the world, it constitutes entering into transgression, for a mind directed toward the world is delusion, whereas one directed beyond the world is wisdom.
A bodhisattva has two vows:

first, the vow that his lying down shall be peaceful and secure, meaning he does not give rise to thoughts of lust; second, the vow that his walking about shall be peaceful and secure, meaning he does not give rise to thoughts of envy, anger, or delusion. These are the two vows.

When a bodhisattva dwells in merit, they loathe merit; when they dwell in transgression, they guard against transgression. Although both merit and transgression must not be abandoned, one should simply recognize them.
If a bodhisattva does not recognize their past lives, they shall not attain Buddhahood.
Why is this? Because they do not recognize their offenses or transgressions.

A bodhisattva does not perform the deeds that lead to the three evil realms; only after fully expiating the karmic retributions of the three evil realms does one attain *avaivartika* (non-retrogression). A bodhisattva can calculate the extent of the offenses leading to the three evil realms, and only after a full hundred kalpas does one attain Buddhahood.
Once a Bodhisattva has received the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), the ninety-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) all remain, yet they are merely attenuated. Why is this?

Because [the Bodhisattva] remains entirely within the practice of a Bodhisattva, contemplating the five destinies of the ten directions with the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) and desiring to bring them to liberation. Even when one offers oneself as food to a starving tigress, gives flesh to a hawk, or sacrifices one's own life for the sake of a living person—acts performed to fulfill the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*)—the fetters are not yet entirely eliminated; they are severed only upon attaining Buddhahood.
When a bodhisattva is able to give away his wife and children, or even his own head to others, what kind of intention does he thereby attain?
There are two causes and conditions for this:

first, he reflects that he does not wish to cause others to feel anger; second, by giving it to them, he enables that person to attain a concentrated mind (*samādhi*), whereas by not giving it, he would cause that person’s mind to become distracted.
Lustful desire carries guilt, while anger carries a heavy offense; fearing that the person might become angry, [the Bodhisattva] offers his head, wife, and children to him.
There are three reasons why a Bodhisattva uses his body to feed a starving tigress or severs his own head to give to others:
first, he reckons that the body must inevitably be abandoned, and thus he uses it for giving as a means of practicing merit.

Second, it is like avenging a grudge: when an enemy dies, one feels joy; the Bodhisattva knows that all evils arise from the body and that various sufferings and calamities are all obtained through the body. Having reckoned it thus, he does not wish to see it, for the body is like an enemy; for this reason, he does not cherish it.
Third, it is because he desires to fulfill his vigor and swiftly attain the path of merit.
When a bodhisattva gives their head, eyes, wife, or children to others:
first, not being attached to forms with the eyes is the "giving away of the eyes";
as for giving the head to others, it means that whenever evil arises, one immediately stops it—this is the "severing of the head."
The wife gives [these] in order to eliminate greed, hatred, and delusion.
There are two aspects to the practice of the Path: first, comparison; second, calculation.
They were weighed for their relative gravity and calculated for their quantity.

A bodhisattva who receives a prediction (vyākaraṇa) undergoes one hundred kalpas; during this time, he practices as a śramaṇa for one kalpa and remains a layperson (avadātavasana) for ninety-nine kalpas.
When a bodhisattva gives away his wife and children to others and sees them being beaten, he considers only their flesh and bones and does not consider them as "mine," and thus he gives them away.

A bodhisattva seeking Buddhahood must practice according to the Buddha-dharma; it must be attained through the thirty-two marks. One's conduct must accord with the Dharma; one cannot attain the Way of the Buddha through a ruined appearance.
A bodhisattva possesses a single intention of compassion that surpasses dhyāna by a hundredfold.
Although a bodhisattva has three paths while in the world, they do not fall into those three paths.
For what reason are they drawn predominantly toward the human and celestial realms?
Because the three paths are not attained, one no longer falls into the three paths; when the three matters of body, speech, and mind are exhausted, the three paths are also exhausted.

The Bodhisattva, being detached from the five paths, always possesses wisdom and merit. When a person dies, there must be a division into the five paths; the Bodhisattva, moreover, possesses the division of wisdom, whereby he immediately knows the distance of his mindfulness.
The Bodhisattva knows that his portion lies with the Srotāpanna and the Sakṛdāgāmin, but his portion does not lie with the Anāgāmin. Why is this?
Because he no longer returns.

In a single Buddha-field, there are three thousand great thousandfold world systems; the births and deaths of humans pervade these worlds, such that there is not even a hair’s breadth that is not included within them. There is nothing they have not done, with the sole exception of not yet having attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) or *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner); all other [karmic deeds] have been undergone countless times.
When the Buddha was a bodhisattva, he gave rise to this thought:
"By what causes and conditions of conduct can one obtain the utmost merit in the present life?
Thus, he further attained the knowledge of past lives through these three types of conduct:
Generosity arises from restraint and from communal assembly.
There are two types of generosity:
first, the gift of the Dharma; second, the gift of material things.
Guarding the body, speech, and consciousness constitutes the charioteer; guarding the mind constitutes the gathering together.

Furthermore, through the causal conditions of giving (*dāna*), one attains liberation and severs greed; through restraint, one severs ill will and a distracted mind; through self-guarding through gathering, one severs delusion.
From generosity one also attains right intention; from restraint one attains right speech; from concentration one attains peace in mental conduct.
Through generosity one perceives the blessing of generosity; through restraint one speaks of the blessing of mindfulness; through concentration one speaks of the blessing of the mind.

The reason a bodhisattva practices giving is that wherever they may be within the five realms of existence, they always abound in joy; they differ from ordinary people in that they immediately attain the status of a king, possessing wisdom and a constant heart of compassion. Having merely exhausted their karma through this, they do not create further karma; thus, even while amidst the conditions for transgression, they do not commit offenses.

It is the same for humans: when a bodhisattva dwells together with his wife and children, he ages twenty-five years in a single day, thirty years in a single month, and fifty-one years in a hundred days.
A bodhisattva merely restrains evil, not the household.
One whose mind is distracted is called a transgressor; because of this lack of tranquility, they should avoid such states from afar.

A mind free from distraction constitutes merit; although living at home is like being in prison, one should simply remain aware of transgressions and no longer find pleasure in the places where they arise. Thus, one is a bodhisattva.
If a person seeking the Way cannot endure humiliation and lacks fortitude, they may yet attain the stage of *srotāpanna*.
The Buddha spoke thus regarding the Bodhisattvas of past lives:
"The Buddha-way is difficult to attain."
"A single word [of praise] reduces [the kalpas by] forty.

By feeding his own body to a starving tiger, he emerged nine kalpas ahead of all other bodhisattvas; having received the prediction (vyākaraṇa) for the sake of Viśvantara, all who practice the path with diligent application shall attain Buddhahood."
There are women who do not attain the Buddha-way.
When a Bodhisattva dwells at home, he has a wife. Why is this?
Because he attained Buddhahood by abandoning his wife and children for six years, he then realized the Way of the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva reckons that wife and children are enemies. Why is this?

To cause others suffering, to increase others' vexation, to disturb others' minds, and to augment others' transgressions—by following after craving and love, one fails to see the Path; for this reason, [craving] is an enemy.

One should regard one's wife and children as if they were enemies; do not follow after craving and attachment. To recognize the mind as soon as it arises is "mindfulness of the mind" (cittasmṛtyupasthāna).
This applies equally to all possessions and even to one's own body.
In the heavens above and on the earth below, throughout the ten directions, all that exists is fire. Why is this?
Because fire already exists.
There are four causes and conditions for a bodhisattva to take a wife:

first, sharing merit from past lives; second, the completion of karmic retribution; third, the necessity of jointly procreating sons and daughters; and fourth, that a wise person who takes a wife may more swiftly attain the Way. If these four conditions do not exist, he does not take a wife.
One who practices the bodhisattva path, with the intention of severing the three poisons of all people throughout the ten directions, therefore attains the Way of the Buddha;
whereas some practice the Way merely desiring to sever their own three poisons, and thus become arhats.
The Bodhisattva destroys his own delusion and likewise destroys the delusion of people throughout the ten directions;
the Arhat destroys his own delusion but does not destroy the delusion of others.
The Bodhisattva possesses great awakening and extensively teaches others to enable them to practice the Path; this is what is meant by destroying the delusion of others.
To be concerned for the people of the ten directions throughout the world is to practice the path of a bodhisattva;
to concern oneself only with one's own body and not think of the people of the ten directions is the path of an arhat.
The Bodhisattva destroys evil, whereas the Arhat does not destroy evil.
The Bodhisattva teaches people the sūtras and precepts, causing them to follow the Dharma of the Path; this is what constitutes destroying evil.
The Arhat maintains himself alone; therefore, it is said that he does not destroy evil.
The Bodhisattva severs suffering for himself and also severs the suffering of people throughout the ten directions; this is what constitutes attaining the Buddha-way.
The Arhat severs suffering for himself but does not sever the suffering of others; therefore, he becomes an Arhat.

The reason why those practicing the bodhisattva path may instead attain the state of an arhat is that they contemplate the Buddha-way as having a cycle of birth and death beyond counting; thinking that all that is to be accomplished must be attained, yet considering this task to be too difficult, they turn toward the stage of an arhat.

Furthermore, they calculate that an Arhat no longer repays their karmic debts and will not undergo further birth and death, but directly attains transcendence; for this reason, they turn toward the state of an Arhat.
Without such thoughts, without the transition of death, and without avoiding suffering, one must surely attain the Buddha-way.

Both Bodhisattvas and Arhats practice according to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the reason they attain Buddhahood is that they maintain the four intentions which Bodhisattvas constantly practice.
What are the four? First, having fortunately attained the karma of a Buddha and encountered a Buddha’s wisdom, I must surely cultivate myself as a Buddha would;

second, constantly maintaining a compassionate intention toward the ten directions, exerting all my strength from that compassionate mind without ever departing from it, so as to liberate the humans and non-humans of the ten directions.
Third, his original supreme vow toward the Buddha remains unshakable in his mind;
fourth, he vows to seek the Way and protect the precepts while remaining in the world, teaching others to increase their wisdom and await the appointed time.
Because one possesses these four intentions, one attains Buddhahood; because one lacks these four intentions, one becomes an Arhat.
Since the intentions of a Buddha and others are identical, there are not two distinct paths; one simply attains results according to the practice of one's own will.
Following after craving, one is bound within the five realms of existence and cannot escape; there is then aging, illness, death, and sorrow, and one is joined with suffering.
When the mind does not follow craving, it is like holding water to extinguish fire;
when it follows craving, it is like holding fuel to increase the fire.
One should contemplate with clarity; by following the truth, one attains the Way.
There are four causes and conditions for a Bodhisattva to take a wife:

first, fearing that others might say he cannot obtain a wife and thus practices the Way; second, fearing that others might say he is solitary and without wife or children and thus practices the Way; third, because the roots of his past lives have not yet been exhausted; and fourth, because evil associates urge him to take a wife.
The Bodhisattva also severs the five aggregates, yet does not sever them.
What is meant by "severing"?
It refers to severing the five burgeoning aggregates and the twelve links of dependent origination.
"Uninterrupted" means that when a bodhisattva is engaged in walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) and follows the path according to its conditions, this is what is meant by "uninterrupted.
The bodhisattva exhausts all offenses and fully attains the Way.
The bodhisattva possesses four kinds of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*):
First, not taking the money of others; second, not violating the wives of others; third, not engaging in double-tongued speech; fourth, not being envious.
The Bodhisattva has severed the three evil realms; he merely remains within them without falling into them.
The Bodhisattva has not yet given rise to the three poisons;
at the stage of a Buddha, there are no three poisons, for the three poisons arise only through the presence of causes and conditions.

The Bodhisattva sat in meditation for six years; as he was about to attain the Way, the three poisons arose simultaneously, and the latent tendencies of lust, anger, and delusion caused his mind to think:
"Has Devadatta taken my wife?"
"Will he surpass me? Will he perhaps take possession of my property?
As these thoughts arose, they were immediately stilled.
"I have severed these three evils since incalculable kalpas ago.
Why is this? Because by further contemplating their cessation, one immediately attains the Way.
The Bodhisattva sat in meditation for six years, consuming only one grain of rice and one grain of hemp each day; this was due to four causes and conditions:
first, to sever craving; second, to exhaust his karmic retribution; third, to demonstrate that he was not hungry; and fourth, to subdue hunger.
He was determined not to eat, thinking that while people attain the Way through hunger, he feared they might instead starve to death.

When the Bodhisattva sat in practice for six years, eating only one grain of rice and one seed of hemp a day, he entered the water to bathe and fell to the ground, unable to rise. A deva then pressed down the branch of a tree until it drooped low; he immediately grasped it and rose up.
There are four causes and conditions for which the Bodhisattva sat beneath the tree for six years without being disturbed by insects, snails, mosquitoes, or gadflies:

first, his fundamental practice of non-killing throughout incalculable lifetimes; second, his cultivation of an impartial mind; third, the protection of devas, ghosts, and spirits; and fourth, the power of the Way being so strong that it also rendered the environment pure.
Bodhisattvas have four things that they do not accumulate:

first, they do not accumulate acts of giving; second, they do not accumulate the hearing of sutras; third, they do not accumulate purity; and fourth, they do not accumulate the performance of meritorious deeds.
When the Bodhisattva first left his home to practice the Way, the great men said to him,
"Now that the Prince lived at home, for what reason have you departed? The Prince replied:
"I have departed because of the three kinds of suffering.
What are these three sufferings?
They are old age, sickness, and death."
The Great Man spoke again:
"Aging, illness, and death are constant matters; why do you depart?
The Prince replied:
"Having contracted this one illness, I am forever unhappy; what shall I ever do?
When the Bodhisattva was born, he walked seven steps upon the ground and stopped, raising his right hand and saying:
"I am the teacher of the heavens above and the world below."
He stopped and did not proceed further.
When the Bodhisattva was a prince, while practicing his studies and going to the teacher’s house, the teacher asked him:
"What do you wish to learn?"
The prince said,
"I wish to study the sixty kinds of scripts.
The teacher asked:
"What are these sixty kinds of scripts?
The Prince then explained them to his teacher in successive order.
The teacher said:
"I know only one kind of script; I am unable to know all other scripts.
The Prince said, "Teach me according to what you know, Master."
Having received the teacher’s instruction, he said,
"This is short by two characters.
The teacher then received those two characters from him once more.
The teacher said, "The Prince already knows such things; why should he learn from me?
The Prince replied:
"Even so, there must be a teacher’s instruction.

When the Bodhisattva had first left the household life and traveled for a hundred *li*, he removed his upper garments and precious jewels, entrusting them to Chandaka to take back; the noble steed Kanthaka shed tears and licked his feet.
Chanda said, "May no one ever have such a wish as this.
The Prince replied:
"The world is deluded; there is no one like you. Why is this?
In this world there are only old age, sickness, death, and the sorrows of suffering; what could you possibly wish for?"
Like a prisoner within a jail, who could find joy?
While one has not yet escaped this state, one further aspires: "When shall I be liberated?
For example, if a hunter’s prey were caught in a net and managed to escape, would it ever think of returning to the net, rather than thinking of its liberation?

Just as one who has escaped from a net never returns to it, I have long contemplated this since my time at home; this intention has existed within me for countless kalpas, not merely brought about by today alone.
There are four causes and conditions for the mother of a Bodhisattva to pass away seven days after his birth:
first, because she bore the Bodhisattva, devas came to watch over her and provide her with food;
second, according to the law of birth and death, one ought to pay homage to one's mother, yet because the Bodhisattva is so venerable, the mother passes away on the seventh day.
Third, it is because his mother’s past karma naturally ordained it so;
fourth, it is like a person who, having performed meritorious service, deserves a fief and is consequently born in heaven.
When the Bodhisattva had not yet attained the Way of the Buddha, he had five dreams:
First, using Mount Sumeru as a pillow;
second, using the earth as a bed;
third, covering the waters of the ocean with one's hand.
Fourth, although there is excrement everywhere under heaven, walking upon it does not soil one's feet;
fifth, a tree grows before one’s heart, reaching up to twenty-seven days [of growth].
To have Mount Sumeru as one’s pillow means that among all those above and below heaven, none is more venerable than the Buddha;
to take the earth as one’s bed means that the Buddha’s body can extend upward as far as the twenty-eighth heaven;
to cover the waters of the ocean with one’s hand means that among all who preach the Way of the sutras, none is superior to the Buddha.
That one walks upon excrement without defiling one's feet signifies that among all the desires of the world, none can defile the Buddha’s mind;
that trees grow before his heart signifies that the Buddha’s words are heard as far up as the twenty-seventh heaven.
There are four causes and conditions by which a bodhisattva associates with women:

first, to exhort women to be diligent; second, because he also wishes to lead women to follow the practice; third, because they encounter one another due to residual karma from countless past lives; and fourth, because of a vow made in a previous existence to teach women.
The devas test bodhisattvas for three reasons:
first, that when they are about to attain Buddhahood, they will have nothing to covet or cherish;
second, should a bodhisattva give rise to such thoughts, [the devas] immediately say to them:
"You shall attain the Way of the Buddha; why then do you act contrary to this?
Because of these words, the Bodhisattva increased his diligence.
Thirdly, because he was destined to attain the marks of a Buddha and would need to be tested, [the deity] went to test him.

While Bodhisattvas practice the six pāramitās, Arhats also practice these same six matters; yet the reason they do not constitute [the state of] "pāramitā" is that Arhats possess only *dāna* (generosity), but lack the pāramitās.
*Dāna* means giving alms; *pāra* means crossing over birth and death; and *mita* means being without limit.
Arhats practice all forms of giving but do not vow to cross over those in the ten directions; therefore, they possess only *dāna*.
Bodhisattvas desire to deliver humans and non-humans throughout the ten directions; therefore, they possess *pāramitā*.
All six matters are likewise so.

When the Buddha was a bodhisattva, wishing to offer food to a buddha, he placed five small beans into the Buddha’s alms bowl; one bean fell to the ground. Later, he became a Golden Wheel-Turning King for eighty lifetimes, ruling over the four continents of the world, because he obtained the merit of those four beans.
As for the bean that did not enter the bowl, he further attained birth as a deva for eight months.
For this reason, there is the dānapāramitā.
When a bodhisattva bestows Dharma-objects upon others, the Buddha’s intention follows the nature of the object and directs his mindfulness so as to bring peace and security to the recipient.
If one gives rise to the thought of wishing to obtain merit, one should then think:
"I shall give to those who are hungry, cold, and poor, so that they may all find peace and security.
This is the giving of the Dharma-method.
Giving a single coin is superior to giving ten million; furthermore, giving even a small amount is superior to giving much, because it employs the mind of the Way to bring about peace and stability.

If, when a person’s life is about to end, their mind dwells upon impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, they shall immediately attain the stage of *avaivartika* and receive their prediction of enlightenment.

If one originally sought arhatship but attained the stage of anāgāmin, it was because the four aspects of impermanence are difficult to realize; yet the reason they were attained is that there was diligent practice in a previous life.
While the Bodhisattva sat in meditation beneath a tree, a crow, a pigeon, and a viper questioned one another:
"What is suffering? The crow said:
"Hunger is the greatest suffering.
How do we know it is suffering?
Because of hunger one cannot walk, nor can one perform any task; people die of starvation. By this, we know that hunger is suffering."
The pigeon said:
"Form alone is suffering.
For what reason do we know that form is suffering?"
"People's mental conceptions of form have no end; all people die because of form. From this we know that form is suffering.
The viper said:
"It is anger alone that is suffering."
For what reason is it known that anger is suffering?
When a person is angry, there is no way to avoid [the consequences]; they wish to kill themselves and also wish to kill others. Therefore, it is known that anger is suffering.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Each of us has spoken of one matter; I shall now speak another for you:
because of speech alone suffering does not arise, yet there is no one who possesses a body and is without suffering."
"This analogy applies to the one hundred and eight modes of craving within a bodhisattva.
When a bodhisattva has not yet attained the Way of the Buddha, there are five teachers:
first, the Nirgrantha; second, the Maudgalyāyana; third, the Ājīvika; fourth, the Rājanya; and fifth, the Rāhula."
When preaching the Dharma of the sutras, one must not accept prostrations. Regarding a bodhisattva who purchases a single verse for five million [pieces of gold], there are three types of purchase:
first, purchasing as a primary acquisition; second, purchasing through repeated exchange; and third, purchasing as a recompense for a gift.
Because a bodhisattva is mindful of kindness, they repay it; the recipient likewise incurs no fault.

Regarding the dharmas practiced by a bodhisattva, they should offer prayers for the people of the ten directions; furthermore, they must maintain a concentrated mind and single-mindedness—if their own mind is not settled, they do not offer such prayers.
Why is this? Because their intention is fixed upon birth and death, their own minds are not settled, and they cannot settle the minds of others.
*Dharma* means "dharma"; *agha* means "the future"; *sa* means "constant"; *parur* means "tears shed"; and *aniruddha* means "life that cannot be numbered."
There are four causes and conditions for why the Bodhisattva Sāpālun constantly sheds tears of compassion:

first, being unable to understand the meaning of the sutras; second, not knowing those who have attained the Way through causes and conditions; third, mindfulness of the people of the ten directions; and fourth, reflecting to himself:
"When shall I attain Buddhahood so as to deliver all beings throughout the ten directions?"
The Bodhisattva said:

"One should maintain wisdom and maintain the mind that knows arising and ceasing; one should practice the Way through non-action, but should simply guard the mind and practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
The reason why one further practices giving and upholds the precepts is that the bodhisattva has compassion for sentient beings.
Although they swiftly sever birth and death, their merit is not yet full; therefore, they practice giving.
In future lives, one does not wish to fall into a poor household; for falling into a poor household means having nothing, which leads to falling into evil conditions.
One who falls into a wealthy household has a peaceful mind and does not follow wickedness; for this reason, one practices giving.
The reason for observing the precepts is that one must have a long life to practice the Way; without a long life, one cannot practice the Way.

Why is this? For instance, if one’s lifespan were only ten years, one would pass away before having attained any knowledge. For this reason, by observing the precept against killing, one attains a long life.

The reason one does not steal is that one constantly reflects that the owner, upon discovering it, will beat them; furthermore, harboring such an evil intention would lead to retribution. For these reasons, one does not steal.
Why does one refrain from double-tongued speech?

The Buddha-way is ultimate sincerity; double-tongued speech is a departure from the Way. In the future, one will not be trusted by the multitude, and even now this can be seen as evil. For these reasons, one refrains from double-tongued speech.
Why is it that one does not engage in sexual misconduct?
It is like facing east: when looking toward the east, one cannot see the west;
if the mind is set on desire, it does not follow the Path. For this reason, one does not engage in sexual misconduct.
Why is it that one does not drink alcohol?

Because when one is intoxicated, one engages in harsh speech, divisive speech, and commits various unwholesome acts; even those who are otherwise skillful and virtuous become disordered in mind. For this reason, one does not drink alcohol.
The Bodhisattva took leave of his parents and went forth to become a śramaṇa.
His parents said,
"What you are doing is perverse."
"A Bodhisattva’s path should be to seek the liberation of all people in the ten directions; now, on the contrary, you have brought sorrow upon your parents.
What kind of thing is this? The Bodhisattva replied, "Because I have sorrow, my parents have sorrow."
Once I have attained the Way, I shall have no sorrow, and my parents will likewise have no sorrow.
It is like when one's relatives have sorrow, one’s own body also sorrows for them.
Again, it is like two people traveling together; if one person has sorrow, the other’s body also sorrows.
"Because the child's sorrow is not resolved, it causes the parents to grieve;
when the child attains the Way, the parents are then liberated from grief.
Then Vimalakīrti addressed the daughter and said to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:

“If Mañjuśrī has already been prophesied as a bodhisattva who practices the foremost profound accordance with conditions, this is because he has deeply transcended causes and conditions; there is no person who follows the practice of causes and conditions.”
Such causes and conditions neither come nor go; they cannot be observed within the eye, nor can they be observed by the mind; they cannot be cognized, nor can they be conditioned.
"If causes and conditions are profoundly deep and severed, they shall be non-existent and without belonging.
Mañjuśrīśrī Bodhisattva then replied:
"That which is fundamentally essential is what constitutes depth."
Vimalakīrti replied again:
"To take that which has no fundamental basis as being without essence—such is it, Mañjuśrī!
Is this not wisdom?"
"Are you not wise? Mañjuśrī replied again,
"What do you mean by this?"
"What should be said? Vimalakīrti replied again,
"One should say that it has already passed."
Mañjuśrī replied again, “The awakened practice of the Tathāgata cannot be perceived through birth and death.
Mañjuśrī then ceased speaking and said no more.
The female bodhisattva Vimaladattā— also known as Niṣkramaṇī— asked Śāriputra,
"Is it because you feel sorrow for me? Śāriputra replied:
"Wise one, most wise one, that which you call 'wise' exists.
If it exists, it must be empty and illusory.
Being illusory, if all such things do not exist, then having no existence, they are not produced."
"Since it has already not arisen, it constitutes a non-common assembly;
if such a thing exists, Śāriputra said: 'There is no wisdom.'"
There was a bodhisattva named Vasumitra who, not understanding a certain *arhat-sūtra*, focused his mind with single-minded intent and went to Maitreya to ask him about it.
Having been asked, he replied to Vāsūmitra,
"I shall explain the matters you have asked about in their proper sequence.
Vāsūmitra, perceiving this, then cross-examined the Arhat.
“Did you just ask Maitreya with a single-minded heart?
The Arhat replied, “Indeed I did.”
There are three causes and conditions for a question arising from a single mind:

first, mutual understanding through the mental faculty; second, a question posed by a manifested body; and third, that which was practiced in previous lives, such that upon hearing it, one immediately understands.
The Bodhisattva Vāsūmitra had recited the three *sūtras* concerning serving one's teacher and the four *Āgamas*. He then took flowers and scattered them over his teacher, saying to him:
"I have already recited the *Catur-āgama-sūtra*."
The Master had forgotten them and could no longer recognize them.
Vāsūmitra then reflected to himself:
"I wish to compile these essential passages from the four Āgamas into a single volume of scripture that may be taught to the four classes of disciples."
When the various practitioners heard the sutra, they were all filled with joy; many came to listen and inquire, yet they did not obtain the opportunity to practice seated meditation.
The practitioners said:

"The reason we listen to the sutras is solely for the sake of practicing the path. Since we have already attained the practice of the path, we should no longer listen to the sutras; we ought simply to depart."
Vasumitra, knowing what was in his mind, placed his hand into the fire without being burned and said,
"Is this not diligent effort?
He then sat upon a large rock.
"There is one who practices the Path while sitting on a soft seat. Vaśumitra said:
"I took up a stone and threw it; before it had even fallen to the ground, I attained Arhatship."
Having leaped upon the rock, he refused to rise; the deva then pulled at the rock from above, preventing it from falling, and said:
"Since you seek the path of a Bodhisattva, we shall all be delivered by you. Twenty kalpas hence, you shall attain the Way of the Buddha; do not destroy your noble resolve."
Among them, a śramaṇa who had not yet attained the Path said,
"This wicked man should not be allowed to remain in the kingdom," and they circulated this message by writing it down and informing one another.
Vasumitra sent someone to request a letter, and the reply read:

"This good man teaches and enlightens others; he does not intend to be self-exalting, but merely fears that evil people might fall into sin. Furthermore, he desires to deliver beings throughout the ten directions, his resolve for the Way being as vast as the sands along the Ganges."

For example, just as the Tathāgatas of the Buddha-lands have no attachment in their perfect enlightenment, what I have spoken should likewise not satisfy the minds of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions; it is a false attainment, for there is no truth to be transgressed, nor is there any "attainment" by a Buddha.
"When a bodhisattva practices four kinds of purification, they shall swiftly attain it. What are these four?
First, purification of persons; second, purification of phenomena; third, purification of the knowable; and fourth, purification of the mind."
Because it exists within the Buddha-land, it is pure; thus, these four purities serve as the means for swift purification.
Furthermore, "the Bodhisattva’s four many-praiseworthy qualities should be swiftly attained."
What are the four? Attachment to the body, attachment to speech, attachment to the mind, and attachment to dwelling—these are the four dharmas of much attachment that lead to swift attainment.

There are also four supports: supporting others to swiftly attain profound patience; supporting others to swiftly attain the signs of excellence known by people; supporting others to know how to practice merit; and supporting others to swiftly attain [the goal]. These are the four supports for making good disciples swiftly attain [their aim] through supporting others.
Śāriputra said: “As it is in the Buddha’s mind, regarding what you have asked and what you contemplate as the pure conduct of a bodhisattva, there is no other wisdom [than this].

To the south there are various bodhisattvas; the city surrounding them is sixteen thousand li in circumference. Within it is the most honored bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, who has instructed countless others who have already attained Buddhahood. His virtue is ten times that of the bodhisattva Dharmākara, and the city is composed entirely of the seven treasures.”
The city where the Bodhisattva Dharmākara dwells is sixteen thousand li in circumference, and its ground is composed entirely of the seven treasures.
Among the bodhisattvas in the northern direction, there was a bodhisattva named Śākyamuni, whose virtue was second only to that of the Bodhisattva Dharmākara.

Regarding the Buddha’s eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*): from the initial attainment of unsurpassed perfect awakening until the attainment of world-transcending *nirvāṇa* without remainder, they are heard to persist until the very end.
First, the Tathāgata’s conduct is without error; second, the Tathāgata’s conduct is without leakage;
third, the Tathāgata’s mental conduct is without forgetfulness; fourth, the Tathāgata’s conduct is never apart from meditative concentration.
Fifth, the Tathāgata’s practice is irreversible; sixth, the Tathāgata’s practice is the contemplation of inexhaustible non-obstruction;
seventh, the Tathāgata’s practice fulfills all intentions; eighth, the Tathāgata’s practice of diligence never diminishes;
ninth, the Tathāgata’s practice of mindfulness does not cease; tenth, the Tathāgata’s...
Eleventh, the Tathāgata’s practice of wisdom is peerless; twelfth, the Tathāgata’s practice of the contemplation of liberation that transcends the world leaves nothing remaining;
thirteenth, the Tathāgata’s practice of knowing past dharmas is immeasurable; fourteenth, the Tathāgata’s practice of knowing the future.

Fifteenth, the Tathāgata’s practice is that there is no extreme; sixteenth, the Tathāgata’s practice is that he fully knows all that is turned by the body of pervasive wisdom regarding the present without error;
seventeenth, the Tathāgata’s practice is that what is spoken by his sharp wisdom is not divorced from consciousness; eighteenth, the Tathāgata’s practice is that he possesses dispersed wisdom.
The mind is detached from discursive thought; this constitutes the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).
*Weiriruzananjing* (Sūtra on the Difficulty of Mixing with the World), one fascicle.
